title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees in AI efficiency push
content:
Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below.
Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.
Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. That put a strain on Microsoft's finances. In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees.
"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees. "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program."
Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation, increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use. It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results. At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities.
The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft's financial profile. In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.
Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added.
More than 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoft said in July. But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.
On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results.

report.summary: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 eligible employees, roughly 27% of its workforce, to balance costly AI infrastructure spending with capital efficiency.
report.background: Microsoft has been spending heavily on data centers to meet AI computing demand from customers including OpenAI and Anthropic. That build-out is straining finances even though Microsoft remains cash-flow positive. In April, the company launched its first voluntary retirement program; in July, it announced 4,800 layoffs. Microsoft is also shifting its business model toward charging customers based on actual AI usage and giving employees AI tools to improve productivity. The buyout program is part of a broader effort to reshape talent and costs without weakening the company’s financial profile as it competes with Alphabet and Amazon in cloud and AI.
key_points: About 60,000 employees in the U.S., Canada, India and the U.K. are eligible, affecting roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000-person workforce. The offer covers workers at experience level 70 and below, and employees must decide in early December, with participants leaving Dec. 31.

The buyout follows an April voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees could join, with more than 30% uptake. The new offer reaches higher, up to vice president level, and Microsoft says it has no specific target for participation.

Microsoft is trying to control costs while funding AI data centers. In its second quarter, free cash flow was $19.64 billion, down 23% year over year, though rivals Alphabet and Amazon reported negative free cash flow in the same period.

The company is changing how it sells AI, increasingly charging clients for actual usage. It has also deployed AI tools across programming, sales and supply chain work, and says it has seen noticeable results, reshaping which skills and roles it prioritizes.

Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have opted not to participate, suggesting the impact will vary by group. Microsoft is scheduled to report quarterly results Wednesday, giving investors a closer look at AI spending and returns.
report.impact: The move signals that even the strongest AI cloud providers face pressure to align huge infrastructure spending with operating efficiency. For the AI industry, it reinforces that capital discipline is becoming as important as model capability. For developers, Microsoft’s internal AI adoption and usage-based pricing point to more AI-assisted workflows, fewer traditional support roles and stronger demand for AI, data and infrastructure skills. For regular users, the near-term effect may be continued AI features in Microsoft products, but usage-based pricing could make advanced AI services more variable in cost. The buyouts also add to broader tech-sector anxiety about job security as companies redirect budgets toward AI computing.
report.tools: To follow the AI efficiency and infrastructure trend, watch Microsoft’s Azure AI Foundry, GitHub Copilot, Copilot Studio and Microsoft Fabric. Open-source projects worth exploring include vLLM for efficient model serving, Ray for distributed AI workloads, MLflow for model lifecycle management, LangChain for AI application development and Open WebUI for local model interfaces.
